vignette:
He is seventy now, a North American man who has spent most of his adult life on the road, selling industrial supplies to hardware stores and small contractors. He still thinks of himself as a salesperson before anything else: someone who can read a room, put people at ease, remember names, shake hands firmly, and keep moving. Before the assault, he takes pride in being steady and unflappable. His wife jokes that nothing rattles him. He believes her.

The assault happens six years ago, on an early winter evening after a long day of client visits. He stops at a gas station on the edge of town, tired and thinking about the drive home. As he comes out of the convenience store with coffee in one hand and his receipts in the other, two younger men approach him. At first he thinks they are asking for money. Then one of them shoves him hard against the side of his car. The coffee spills down his coat. He remembers the confusion before the fear fully lands: the shock of being touched that way, the strange delay in understanding that this is really happening. One man grabs at his wallet; the other strikes him in the face and ribs when he resists. He falls awkwardly onto the pavement. He can still recall the smell of gasoline, the scrape of gravel under his palm, the sound of one of them cursing at him as if he is the problem. The assault is over in minutes, but what stays with him is the helplessness. He lies there stunned, bleeding from his lip, aware that he is an older man on the ground while strangers decide what to take.

In the emergency room he minimizes it. He says he is lucky. Just bruises, soreness, a cracked pair of glasses. He is more embarrassed than angry. At home, his wife is shaken by the sight of him, but he reassures her and tries to make a story of it, something with a beginning and an end. For a few days he repeats the facts as if repetition will settle them into the past.

Instead, the assault follows him. At night he jerks awake with his heart pounding, convinced for a moment that someone is standing over him. He does not always dream the event exactly; sometimes it is only the pressure of being trapped, the certainty that something bad is about to happen. He begins checking the locks before bed, then checking them again. If he hears footsteps behind him in a parking lot, his shoulders tighten and his body turns before his mind catches up. He finds himself studying young men in hooded sweatshirts, scanning their hands, their distance from him, the way they move. This vigilance feels practical to him at first, even wise. His wife notices that he no longer wants to stop for gas after dark.

Work changes in quieter ways. Sales has always required ease with strangers, but now every unfamiliar parking lot gives him a small jolt. He starts arranging his route so he can be home before evening. He avoids certain neighborhoods entirely, even when they contain longtime accounts. If a customer suggests meeting at a busy café or asks him to come by after hours, he finds a reason to reschedule. He tells himself he is simply getting older and more selective. Still, he notices that he is losing something central to how he has always worked. He used to linger and chat. Now he keeps one eye on the door.

His wife sees more than he says. In restaurants he insists on the seat facing the entrance. In line at the grocery store he becomes tense if someone stands too close behind him. He is quicker to anger than he used to be, especially when he feels cornered or dismissed. Small frustrations-a driver cutting him off, a clerk speaking sharply-can leave him flushed and shaky. Afterward he feels ashamed. He tells himself he should be over this by now. The assault was brief. Other people have survived worse. This private comparison becomes another burden.

What troubles him most is the way the world has narrowed. He still works, still makes his calls, still jokes with customers who have known him for years. On the surface, his life remains recognizable. But inside, he feels less free. Ordinary errands require calculation. Fatigue comes from the constant monitoring: where to park, who is nearby, whether there is a clear exit. Some evenings he sits in his driveway for a few extra minutes before going inside, hands resting on the steering wheel, waiting for his body to understand that he is home.

When he talks about the assault now, he does not dwell on the stolen wallet or the bruises. What he returns to is the moment on the pavement when he realizes he cannot stop what is happening. At seventy, he says, a man expects to know who he is. Since that night, he finds himself living with a version of fear he used to think belonged to other people.
